title: A new hybrid classification algorithm for customer churn prediction based on logistic regression and decision trees
harvard_reference: De Caigny, A., Coussement, K. and De Bock, K.W. (2018) 'A new hybrid classification algorithm for customer churn prediction based on logistic regression and decision trees', European Journal of Operational Research, 269(2), pp. 760-772. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2018.02.009.
abstract_summary: The paper proposes the logit leaf model (LLM), a two-stage hybrid classifier for customer churn prediction: a decision tree first segments customers into homogeneous leaves, then a separate logistic regression is fitted in each leaf. The motivation is that decision trees and logistic regression are both popular in churn prediction because they combine good predictive performance with good comprehensibility, but trees struggle with linear relations while logistic regression misses interaction effects. LLM is benchmarked on fourteen churn datasets from different industries against decision trees, logistic regression, random forests and logistic model trees, using AUC and top-decile lift. LLM scores significantly better than its building blocks (LR and DT) and performs at least as well as the ensemble/advanced methods random forests and logistic model trees. Comprehensibility is demonstrated through a case study with a proposed LLM visualization.

claims_supported.claim: Logistic regression and decision trees are widely used in churn prediction because of their comprehensibility; a hybrid (logit leaf model) can combine accuracy with interpretability.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (first sentence: 'Decision trees and logistic regression are two very popular algorithms in customer churn prediction with strong predictive performance and good comprehensibility'); Introduction, para 3 ('very popular techniques ... because they combine good predictive performance with good comprehensibility (Verbeke et al., 2012)'); Highlights ('designed to perform well in terms of both accuracy and interpretability'); Conclusions ('the LLM is proposed as a viable choice that scores high on both requirements').

claims_supported.claim: In their benchmark on 14 datasets, the logit leaf model was competitive with random forests.
claims_supported.where: Introduction, para 4 ('Fourteen customer churn datasets from different industries are used on which the LLM is benchmarked against ... DT, LR, random forests (RF) and logistic model trees (LMT)'); Section 4 'Data and experimental design' ('Experiments are conducted on fourteen churn datasets originating from different sources. Table 3 provides an overview'); Abstract ('performs at least as well as more advanced ensemble methods random forests and logistic model trees' on AUC and top decile lift). 'Competitive' is a fair paraphrase of 'at least as well as'.

verification_notes: Metadata verified against the CrossRef record for DOI 10.1016/j.ejor.2018.02.009 (title, three authors, container-title European Journal of Operational Research, volume 269, issue 2, pages 760-772, published-print 2018-09, publisher Elsevier BV, ISSN 0377-2217). Cross-checked with OpenAlex (same biblio; publication_date 2018-02-12 = available online) and Semantic Scholar (abstract, DBLP key journals/eor/CaignyCB18, ~482-528 citations). The ScienceDirect landing page (issue dated 1 September 2018, section 'Innovative Applications of O.R.') was read via the built-in browser and provides the Highlights, Abstract, full Introduction and section snippets; the 'fourteen datasets' statement was confirmed there directly, and also independently in a citing paper (Sustainability 2023, doi:10.3390/su15054543, which lists LLM as evaluated on '14 different churn datasets'). The lead reference given was accurate apart from omitting page numbers and the DOI. Full text is paywalled (Unpaywall: no OA copy), so the results tables were not inspected; the random-forest comparison is taken from the abstract and the conclusions snippet.
caveats: The paper uses the term 'comprehensibility' (and 'interpretability' in the Highlights); either wording is acceptable. 'Competitive with random forests' should be phrased as 'performed at least as well as random forests and logistic model trees' to match the authors' wording; the paper does not claim LLM beats random forests. It is not verified from the accessible text which fourteen datasets were used (Table 3 is behind the paywall), so the report should not state that the Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset was among them. The case study uses 'a public dataset' whose identity is not visible in the accessible text.
